be1fcf5c12.q: What are the four Australian tax residency tests and can you fail just one to be non-resident?
be1fcf5c12.a: There are four tests: the resides test based on ordinary concepts, domicile, the 183-day test, and the Commonwealth super test. You only need to meet one of them to be an Australian tax resident, so you must fail all four to be non-resident. The 183-day test is often misunderstood—simply being overseas for more than 183 days does not automatically make you non-resident if you still have strong family and economic ties to Australia.
be1fcf5c12.e: Expat Chat Episode 193 - Aussie Expats in Asia: Residency & Provident Funds
be1fcf5c12.rq: The 183-day test is probably more relevant if you've fully cut ties and been overseas as a non-resident, or when returning to Australia on smaller trips, not for more than half the year.

d8ea2b9a9b.q: What happened in the Pike case regarding tax residency determination in Thailand and Singapore?
d8ea2b9a9b.a: In the Pike case, someone who moved to Singapore and Thailand and marked themselves as non-resident was deemed an Australian tax resident by the courts because their family was still based in Australia and they returned quite frequently. Although they thought they had cut ties, the courts determined they had sufficient ties under the resides test because their centre of life was still partially in Australia, requiring them to unwind all non-resident arrangements and be taxed as an Australian resident.

83e14de735.q: How are Southeast Asian provident funds taxed when withdrawn as an Australian resident?
83e14de735.a: Provident funds in Hong Kong, Malaysia, and other Southeast Asian countries are treated as foreign trusts rather than foreign super funds by the ATO, so they cannot be transferred into an Australian super fund. When withdrawn as an Australian resident, they are taxed as ordinary income at marginal tax rates, though there are some discounts or concessions for contributions that were previously made by you or your employer.

bc134bad65.q: What changed with Thailand tax residency and foreign income remittances from January 1, 2024?
bc134bad65.a: Since January 1, 2024, Thai tax residents can be taxed on foreign income that has been remitted into Thailand from that date onward. This is a significant change that affects many retired Australians moving to Thailand, as they may now face tax on money they bring into the country, whereas previously this was not taxed.

b69463ced6.q: Should you sell your Australian home before moving overseas to utilize the main residence exemption?
b69463ced6.a: Selling your main residence while still an Australian tax resident allows you to utilize the main residence exemption, making the transaction tax-free if it hasn't been rented out for more than six years. If you rent it out first and then sell as a non-resident, you lose the exemption entirely and will pay capital gains tax on the transaction. The decision depends on whether you plan to return to Australia—if uncertain, you could keep it for up to six years under the temporary absence rule and still be tax-free if you move back in.
